input_signals.name: Buyback-Validated Knowledge Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has accumulated a large five-year R&D stock and is simultaneously a net repurchaser of its own shares is telling the market that management views its unbooked knowledge capital as worth more than the traded price; this joint condition identifies undervalued intangible assets rather than hyped ones.
input_signals.reasoning: The multiplicative form requires both conditions at once, so the score is high only for intangible-rich firms that are net-shrinking their equity base—the opposite of market-timed issuance. Accounting expensing of R&D understates book equity, and the repurchase decision acts as an insider validation that the understatement is real.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Issuance Into Fading Intangible Productivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(revt, ADD(intan, MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3))), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: External financing is only value-creating when the firm's existing intangible base is still converting into revenue; firms that raise large amounts of new capital while the revenue generated per dollar of intangible capital is on a multi-year downtrend are financing a decaying franchise or timing an inflated valuation.
input_signals.reasoning: The five-year trend in revenue per unit of intangible capital is a direct measure of intangible productivity, and interacting its deterioration with total external financing separates funded-and-productive innovators from funded-but-unproductive issuers. This is a productivity-conditioned issuance effect, not a restatement of the well-known standalone issuance anomaly, since heavy issuers with improving intangible productivity receive a low (non-negative) score.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( revt, add( intan, ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ) ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unexplained Issuance Beyond Intangible Needs
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(COALESCE(xrd, 0), COALESCE(xad, 0))), at), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: External capital raised is benign when it is matched by contemporaneous intangible outlays (R&D and brand spending) that the firm cannot fund internally, but capital raised far in excess of those outlays is discretionary, opportunistic issuance; the dollar gap between funds raised and intangible investment needs therefore predicts low returns, while firms whose issuance is fully absorbed by innovation spending should not be penalized.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the additive rank-sum with a single dollar-netted "financing surplus" quantity, so two firms with identical issuance receive opposite scores depending on whether the proceeds are matched by intangible investment — a genuine interaction that the standalone issuance or R&D anomalies cannot produce. Firms that issue exactly what they spend on R&D score near zero and sit in the middle of the cross-section, which is precisely the economically neutral "need-driven financing" case.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), coalesce( xad, 0 ) ) ), at ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Capital-to-Knowledge Conversion Ratio
input_signals.expression: RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), TS_SUM(sstk, 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Over a five-year window, a firm either converts outside equity into knowledge capital or it does not: the share of the firm's combined "R&D plus equity raised" pool that actually went into research measures how efficiently external funding is transformed into innovation. Firms near one built their knowledge stock without selling shares, while firms near zero sold large amounts of equity with almost nothing to show for it in intangible investment, and the latter are the market-timers.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the payout-conditioning template entirely: it never signs the level of financing or payout, so it cannot collapse into the net-external-financing anomaly, and a firm that issues heavily but spends all of it on R&D scores as favorably as a non-issuer. The bounded [0,1] construction also eliminates the denominator blow-ups and heavy tails that destabilize ratio signals, which should help the portfolio alpha as well as the cross-sectional slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), add( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), ts_sum( sstk, 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Persistently Self-Funded Innovators
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), at)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 0.01), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of net repurchase can be a one-off event (an ASR, an option-dilution offset, or a lucky window), whereas repeatedly retiring equity in most of the last five years while sustaining a large research stock demonstrates a durable ability to fund innovation out of operating cash flow; persistence, not the dollar size of the latest buyback, is what identifies genuinely productive intangible financing.
input_signals.reasoning: The winning signal's payout leg is a level that is dominated by a handful of very large one-year repurchases, which is a plausible source of portfolio instability (Sharpe 0.49 but t-alpha only 2.8); counting years of net equity retirement is a robust, outlier-immune restatement of the same economic condition. Evaluating both versions isolates a specific design choice — intensity versus persistence — in the leg that carries the mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), at ) ), ts_sum( indicator( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), 0.01 ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Off-Balance-Sheet Knowledge Capital Meets Buybacks
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mispriced quantity is the *dollar amount* of intangible capital a firm has built that never appears on its balance sheet: five years of expensed research minus whatever intangibles have actually been capitalized. When management retires equity while carrying a large positive stock of unrecorded knowledge capital, it is buying back claims on assets that reported book value does not contain, and those firms subsequently outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the composition share with a scaled difference restores the magnitude the hypothesis depends on: a firm with negligible R&D and no recorded intangibles now scores near zero in the middle of the distribution instead of at the maximum, and goodwill-heavy acquirers score negative because their intangible base is already visible. There is no 0/0 denominator since the scaling variable is total assets, so coverage matches the archive's best signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Maturity Squeeze on Research Programs
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Research programs require uninterrupted funding, so a research-dependent firm that simultaneously carries a large near-term debt load and generates little gross profit is exposed to a forced curtailment of innovation when maturities come due; the market underweights this risk because R&D cuts only become visible with a reporting lag.
input_signals.reasoning: The explosive and sign-flipping ratio is gone: both stress channels are now scaled by total assets and combined through SUMRANK, so loss-making research firms score as *more* stressed (high current debt, low or negative gross profit) exactly as the mechanism intends. The multiplicative R&D gate preserves the interaction — refinancing pressure is only damaging here because the firm has an innovation program to sacrifice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), at ) ), sumrank( ratio( dlc, at ), neg( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Issuance Penalty Concentrated in Innovation Leaders
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3), sale)), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that out-spend their industry peers on research are the ones with the most compelling growth narratives and hence the widest scope for valuation-driven issuance; the return penalty for raising outside capital should therefore be strongest precisely among peer-leading innovators, and nearly absent for firms whose research effort is unremarkable relative to their industry.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not an industry-neutralized restatement of an existing signal — the industry rank serves as the *intensity of the penalty*, making the proposal a heterogeneity hypothesis about where the issuance effect lives, with the financing leg entering in signed, winsorized dollar form rather than as a rank. Paired with the low-intensity-researcher signal above, the two proposals make opposite predictions about which side of the innovation distribution drives the issuance penalty, so the batch is informative whichever one wins.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), sale ) ), neg( winsor( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Stress Against Acquired Rather Than Organic Intangibles
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the squeeze effect is really about collateral — intangible assets cannot be pledged or sold quickly — it should appear just as strongly for firms whose intangible base is capitalized acquired intangibles and goodwill; if instead it is about the interruption of an ongoing research program, only organic R&D dependence should matter and this version should be far weaker.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive contains both a failed collateral signal built on `intan` with debt *flows* (fmb -1.5) and a very strong squeeze signal built on R&D with debt *stocks*, so holding the stress composite fixed and swapping only the intangible gate cleanly identifies which economic story generates the alpha. This is a discrimination test whose outcome redirects the remaining search either toward collateral or toward innovation-continuity mechanisms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), at ) ), sumrank( ratio( dlc, at ), neg( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Signed Payout Scaled by Hidden Research Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms carrying large unrecorded research capital, the direction of the capital flow is what separates productive intangible financing from overvaluation-driven issuance: those returning cash to shareholders are validating assets the balance sheet omits, while those raising equity are monetizing a valuation the hidden assets do not justify.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen-3 exposed an identification problem in this family — replacing the buyback leg with equity *issuance* still produced a large positive alpha (+5.1%, t 4.1), which means the [0,1] rank product lets the hidden-capital leg alone build the long portfolio and the financing leg barely signs the spread. Multiplying by a mean-zero, winsorized net-payout z-score forces the short leg to be hidden-capital-rich *issuers* and the long leg hidden-capital-rich *payers*, so any resulting spread is attributable to the interaction rather than to the knowledge-capital premium.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Productive Intangible Base Behind Equity Retirement
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0))), RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Management's decision to retire equity is most informative when the firm holds a large stock of unrecorded research capital *and* that intangible base is demonstrably converting into gross margin; the combination identifies innovation that is both invisible to the balance sheet and commercially proven, which is precisely the productive intangible financing the mandate asks us to separate from hype.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's inversion problem is resolved by requiring both channels in the intangible factor: a low-R&D, high-gross-profit firm now scores high on conversion efficiency but low on hidden capital, so it can no longer dominate the long leg, and the intangible content is restored rather than stripped out. Because the productivity ratio uses the full intangible base (accumulated R&D plus capitalized intangibles) as its denominator, it measures return on intangible capital rather than a rescaled gross-profitability sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ), sumrank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), add( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ), ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Buybacks While Hidden Capital Is Still Building
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: There is an economic difference between a firm retiring equity while its stock of unrecorded research capital is still expanding and one buying back shares as that stock decays: the first is reinvesting and returning cash simultaneously from a live research franchise, the second is harvesting a mature position, and only the former should command a premium.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than widening the financing leg into the published net-external-financing measure, this holds the tested buyback leg fixed and replaces the intangible *level* with its one-year accumulation, which asks whether the archive's best result is a stale value-style stock effect or a live franchise-building effect. That distinction has real consequences for later generations — if accumulation carries the alpha, the search should move toward intangible-capital dynamics rather than static hidden-asset levels.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( delta( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Payout Coverage Alongside a Funded Research Budget
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The credible statement about hidden intangible value is not that a firm repurchased shares, but that it repurchased shares *while continuing to fund its laboratory* — net equity retirement measured per dollar of annual research spending shows whether internal cash flow covers both uses at once, which is exactly the distinction between productive self-financed innovation and cash returned by a firm that has stopped investing.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than averaging two tested signals, this changes the economic content of the financing leg: scaling payout by the research budget rather than by assets makes the leg a statement about the *joint affordability* of investment and distribution, and it automatically restricts the sample to firms that actually run research programs. Because the denominator is the research commitment itself, the two themes are fused inside a single ratio instead of being two independently ranked anomalies.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt-Financed Intangible Acquisition
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's balance sheet intangibles jump in the same year that it takes on net new debt, it has bought innovation rather than built it and has pledged fixed obligations against assets that cannot be repossessed; such deals systematically overpay, and the impairment and refinancing consequences arrive later than the market expects.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive tested this collateral idea only with the intangible *level* (fmb -1.5, alpha -1.3), which is dominated by long-stale acquisitions, whereas the economically active moment is the year the intangible base expands on borrowed money — a distinct event that also avoids the heavily documented stock-financed-acquirer channel. It complements the archive's squeeze results by asking whether debt-funded intangible expansion, not just debt burden, predicts underperformance.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Buybacks at the Peak of the Research Cycle
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Productive intangible financing means investing and distributing at the same time: a firm retiring equity in the very year its research effort stands at a five-year high relative to revenue is demonstrating that internal cash covers an expanding innovation program, whereas an identical buyback made while research is at a cyclical low is a harvest, not a signal of franchise strength.
input_signals.reasoning: Every positive-family entry in the archive measures the intangible leg as a cross-sectional level, which loads heavily on industry membership; replacing it with each firm's own five-year percentile position converts the test into one about the *timing* of the payout relative to the research cycle, a question the archive has never asked. Because the comparison is within-firm, the long portfolio should be far less concentrated in a few research-heavy industries, which is a plausible route to a more reliable FF5 t-alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 5 ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internally Funded Payout Behind Hidden Research Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(prstkc, sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A buyback only validates unrecorded research capital if the cash came from the franchise rather than from lenders; netting new borrowing out of net equity retirement isolates distributions genuinely funded by operations, and it should strengthen the archive's best positive signal by removing the recapitalizations that masquerade as insider confidence.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen 6 produced direct evidence for this correction: intangible-heavy firms that simultaneously paid out and borrowed (the MIN construction) earned a *negative* FF5 alpha of -3.2% (t -2.5), so those firms are currently sitting in the long leg of the champion signal and dragging it down. This is therefore not a broadening of the payout leg into the published net-financing measure but a targeted removal of a subgroup the archive has independently shown to be harmful.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( sub( sub( prstkc, sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Brand Capital Validated by Equity Retirement
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xad, 0), 5), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Advertising builds customer and brand capital that is expensed and therefore invisible in exactly the same way research is; if the archive's premium reflects accounting invisibility rather than technology, consumer-facing firms with large accumulated advertising stocks that retire equity should earn a comparable premium.
input_signals.reasoning: Every intangible leg tested so far is research-based, so the archive cannot say whether the mechanism is about R&D specifically or about expensed intangibles generally — an unresolved question with direct consequences for how the final signal should be built. Because advertising reporters are concentrated in consumer industries, a positive result would also give the long portfolio an industry composition very different from the current technology- and pharma-heavy tilt, which would improve diversification of the spread.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xad, 0 ), 5 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Retirement Rate of the Invisible Asset Base
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically informative quantity is not how much cash a firm returns relative to its books but how fast it is buying in the claim on its invisible research assets: net equity retired per dollar of accumulated knowledge capital measures the pace at which management is concentrating ownership of assets the market cannot see, and a high retirement rate is the strongest available statement that those assets are worth more than the price.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a targeted repair of the archive's highest-ever cross-sectional slope: gen 5 normalized payout by the *annual* research budget and produced fmb 5.91 but only 5.2% coverage and no alpha, because a one-year R&D denominator is small, volatile and available for few firms. Normalizing instead by the five-year knowledge stock keeps the same economic ratio, roughly doubles coverage, and stabilizes the extreme portfolios, while the hidden-capital leg supplies the abnormal-return engine the earlier version lacked.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Counterparty Versus Capital-Market Funding of Innovation
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3), at)), SUB(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), LAG(at, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mandate's central question — productive intangible financing versus market-timed issuance — is answered most cleanly by asking who is funding the research program: when a firm's innovation is increasingly financed by customers and suppliers it reflects demand for the product, whereas when it is financed by fresh equity and debt it reflects only the willingness of investors to buy a story.
input_signals.reasoning: This puts the archive's two best-identified financing channels in direct opposition inside one mean-centred term, so the long leg is research firms pulled forward by counterparty credit and the short leg is research firms pushed along by capital-market issuance — a contrast no existing entry makes. Because the financing factor is a signed rank difference rather than a [0,1] rank, the spread must be signed by the funding source rather than by the R&D level, which is the identification lesson the archive learned in gen 4.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), at ) ), sub( rank( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Substitution Toward Counterparty Credit by Researchers
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), lt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A research firm whose claim structure is shifting away from lenders and toward ordinary business counterparties is replacing hard, dated obligations with soft ones; this substitution reduces the probability that the innovation program is interrupted by a refinancing event, and it typically happens because commercial partners have become more willing to transact on credit.
input_signals.reasoning: Measuring the change in the non-debt *share* of liabilities rather than the growth of the non-debt liability dollar amount removes the scale component that makes the gen-7 construction resemble the liability side of the accruals anomaly, since a firm can score high here while its total liabilities shrink. Paired with the level version, the two proposals separate the persistent state of counterparty-financed operations from the transition into it, which is the specific question the gen-7 surprise left open.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), at ) ), rank( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), lt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capital Markets Replacing Withdrawn Trade Credit
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), LAG(at, 1)), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), lt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a research firm's counterparties tighten terms, the shortfall has to be replaced from somewhere; firms that plug the gap by selling securities are substituting patient, informed commercial credit with impatient, uninformed capital-market money, and the very parties closest to the business are the ones voting against it.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the payout-scaling family the critic judged exhausted and instead tests a substitution event — outside capital raised precisely as counterparty credit recedes — which no archive entry examines, since the accepted companion signal pairs counterparty withdrawal with the *stock* of maturing debt rather than with new issuance. Both financing channels enter through equally weighted ranks with no profitability term anywhere, so the result is attributable to the funding-source substitution itself.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ma( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), at ) ), sumrank( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), lag( at, 1 ) ), neg( delta( ratio( sub( lt, add( dltt, dlc ) ), lt ), 1 ) ) ) )
